newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian jobs data confuses rates outlook.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian jobs data confuses rates outlook.

text.p: Australian markets on Thursday were faced with the baffling combination of stronger employment growth and a higher unemployment rate as the latest clue to the next move in official interest rates.
The Bureau of Statistics reported that employment rose by 37,900 in August against median expectations of an 11,000 rise.
However, included in the total were the 10,000 temporary jobs created by the collection of the national census.
Despite the jump in employment, the unemployment rate rose to 8.8 percent, after the market had expected it to remain at the July level of 8.5 percent.

Economists found signs of both strength and weakness in the data to support arguments either for the Reserve bank to deliver another rate cut or hold policy steady, although most seemed to feel another cut was a definite possibility
"It's a bit baffling. There is very strong employment growth and a higher unemployment rate," Bankers Trust Australia chief economist Chris Caton said.
"My disposition is always to place more importance on the unemployment rate, so you can't claim that this is a strong report," Caton said.
But some did see the report as strong. Bain and Co associate director Ivan Colhoun said removing the census workers still left jobs growth at about 28,000 in the month.
"This is another strong number among a string of strong numbers recently," Colhoun said, noting it followed strong retail sales, housing finance and credit data.

"Most of this data preceeds or is coincident with the last rate cut which the RBA described as a confidence booster," Colhoun said. "It would seem the chances of another cut are somewhat less than some people are saying," he said.
Generally, however the reaction was more cautious.
"They were a bit of a mixed bag," Citibank Australia chief economist Grant Bailey said of the data.
"If they (the RBA) still have a bias towards easing, it doesn't move them any further towards an easing, and it doesn't move them away from that either," he said.

Macquarie Bank senior economist John Kyriakopoulos said excluding the census workers, the data still showed "a medium rise in employment and may at the margins make it a little less likely the RBA will cut rates again if this employment growth is maintained for the rest of the year."
"But we still think there could be another rate cut," he said.
Other economists said that while the headline rise in employment suggested strength, the rise in full-time employment of only 11,200 suggested ongoing weakness.

"The full-time growth is a better indicator of the underlying trend," ANZ senior Treasury economist David de Garis said. "The growth is consistent with the pattern of the last three months, nothing has changed very much ... we still believe the door is ajar for another easing."
With unemployment pushing upwards in the month, the likelihood of it remaining high or even moving to above 9.0 percent, would also keep a rate cut firmly on the agenda.

"If wages are under control, inflation is low and the unemployment rate is high, a strong case can be made for lower interest rates this year," State Bank of New South Wales chief economist Hans Kunnen said.
